world.org_type: nonprofit regional health system with three hospitals and an employed medical group, replacing commercial occurrence professional liability policies with a self-insured claims-made trust

driver: A cover that pays only for events first reported inside its own short window is priced from a history in which the process that makes the quickest reports, and the costliest of those a short window catches, began part way through, unit by unit on each unit's own date, and has run steadily since; the window inherits that process, so its expected cost is each past event's own cost counted for the exposure from which its own delay still lands it inside the window, taken on each unit's history from its own start, which neither the whole history's loss-weighted report pattern, nor the count of events that would report in time at an average or a fitted cost, gives.
driver_concrete: Each hospital and the employed medical group joins the new trust, claims-made, on the day its occurrence policy expires, so the 2027 cost is the Claims first made by 31 December 2027 from incidents after each entity's Transition Date; those are mostly the harm the care team discloses and the Early Resolution Program settles within weeks, at tens of thousands, with program requests a few months on settled for a few thousand, while the demands and suits made a year or more on carry nearly all the experience's cost. The disclosure settlements began at each entity in the first half of 2019 (none from 2016 to 2018 incidents) and run every year since, so the window is costed on each entity's experience from its first settlement, each Claim at its own trended cost against the 2027 FTE-years of its class with its own delay still left, not on the whole 2016 to 2024 experience the trust holds ($1,000,000), nor at the window's expected count times the class average ($3,250,000) or the within-a-year average ($1,000,000).
stump: A strong solver who reads the claims-made window correctly and prices it the field's way, each 2016 to 2024 Claim at its own trended cost against the 2027 FTE-years with its own delay left (the loss-weighted claims-made step factor), files $1,000,000 ($961,261 unrounded); the step that lands it there is pooling the whole experience the trust holds, when the Claims a first claims-made year catches are mostly the Early Resolution Program's disclosure settlements, made within weeks, which began at each entity only between January and July 2019 and have run every year since: 2016 to 2018 carry the program's requests and the late suits but none of the settlements, so they understate the window by a quarter; costing the window on each entity's experience from its first settlement gives $1,250,000, and the count route at the class average misses on either experience ($3,250,000 and $3,750,000).
analyst_test: a strong analyst who dedupes the register, merges each incident's claim numbers, reads the claims-made window and costs every window Claim at its own delay (the loss-weighted step factor, claim by claim or by month) still files $1,000,000 on the whole 2016 to 2024 experience ($961,261 on the generator's clean truth, asserted), a full bin and more below the golden $1,250,000; the frequency-severity route misses on either experience ($3,750,000 on the whole, $3,250,000 since the starts); only the experience since each entity's first disclosure settlement, costed at each Claim's own delay, lands.
domain_test: the deciding quantity is the expected cost of claims first made inside a claims-made trust's opening window, built from each entity's covered exposure through the system's own report-lag experience, each claim at its own cost and lag, on the experience period that matches the claims process the window will run under, which is how a professional liability actuary prices a first claims-made year after a change in claims handling; with another field's nouns (a warranty, a subscription) there is no claims-made trigger, retroactive date, disclosure settlement or late suit for the cost and its timing to depend on.

differentiation.task102: task102 moves payments across a period boundary by a business-day release rule; here nothing moves across a boundary: a claims-made window keeps only the claims made soon after their incident, which are the cheap early-resolution ones, so the cost is the exposure at each point of each entity's months of cover times the cost of past claims made within the time then left.
differentiation.task501: task501 v3 sized a buffer on the furthest a cumulative path ran ahead of its forecast inside a test horizon; here no path maximum or buffer is involved: the cost of a claims-made opening window is a lag-truncated, cost-weighted share of exposure, entity by entity.
differentiation.task134: task134 v2 round 2 forecasts a pool's inflow over a window holding an announced threshold step, the step's size scaled from a smaller one the history holds; here no threshold steps and nothing is scaled: a claims-made opening window keeps only the claims made soon after their incident, the cheap early-resolution ones, so the cost is each day's covered exposure times the trended cost of past claims made within the days then left.
differentiation.task130: v4 round 1's decisive step was the claims-made window itself; round 3a made the truncation the default and decided on each window claim's own cost at its own lag, which the field's loss-weighted step factor reaches without seeing it; round 3b keeps both and decides on the experience period: the disclosure settlements that dominate the window began at each entity in 2019, so the step factor on the whole 2016 to 2024 experience misses by a bin. Round 2 split the history by unit (the program's hospitals against the rest, every year pooled); here every unit's own history is used, each from its own start, and no filed sentence defines the experience as a pool.

lineage.driver: Members of a closed group leave only when a rationed supply reaches them, and the supply is handed out across a wider list in a filed priority order within each size class, so how many remain at a later date is each member's rank inside its class against the cumulative planned supply, and neither a leaving rate nor a survival curve read off history, which both average over whatever list length the past happened to have, gives it.
